---
title: "How do you make your work easier to review?"
last-reviewed: "2026-08-28"
---

Sending a document with “any thoughts?” makes the reviewer guess whether you want help with the argument, the method, the structure or the commas. The result is often late, contradictory or pitched at the wrong level. A review contract names the state of the work, the decision you need, the questions the reviewer should answer and the deadline. It also makes clear what is outside scope. Reviewable work is not necessarily polished; it is organised so another person can inspect the right thing.

## Tell the reviewer what decision the draft must support

Make the work reviewable for a named decision. State the purpose, audience, maturity, checks already completed, known gaps, feedback requested, material that is deliberately unfinished and the agreed response window. After review, translate comments into underlying issues and record a reasoned disposition.

Feedback is evidence for a revision decision—not an instruction stream to obey blindly or reject defensively. The student should understand, test and own the resulting argument while respecting decisions that belong to formal authorities.

## Choose the review level

| Level | Useful question | Material to provide | Usually premature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direction | Is this the right question, contribution or route? | one-page case, options and recommendation | sentence editing |
| Argument | Does the reasoning support the claim? | argument map and representative evidence | formatting polish |
| Structure | Can the reader follow the chapter's jobs and sequence? | full skeleton or developmental draft | isolated word choice |
| Method or analysis | Is the design, implementation or inference defensible? | protocol, code/output, deviations and exact questions | broad “thoughts?” request |
| Reporting | Is the account complete, accurate and bounded? | substantive draft and reporting checks | cosmetic refinement |
| Copy and production | Is the final expression and package correct? | stable near-final version | major conceptual redesign |

Do not ask for every level simultaneously unless the reviewer has agreed to a full review and sufficient time.

## Create a review contract

Before sending consequential work, agree or state:

- exact file, version and authoritative location;
- purpose and intended reader;
- draft maturity;
- the decision the review should support;
- one to three priority questions;
- checks already completed;
- known gaps and material excluded from review;
- expected depth and format of response;
- realistic review window and decision date; and
- where responses and decisions will be recorded.

::: {.decision-card}
**Smallest useful next action:** Add a cover note that lets a busy reviewer understand the decision, state and requested response without first reading the entire draft.
:::

If timing matters, ask before sending a large package. “Can you review a 9,000-word full chapter for argument and structure by 18 September?” is a request that can be accepted, renegotiated or declined. “Please send feedback soon” hides the dependency.

## Make the work inspectable

A reviewable package should allow the reader to:

1. identify what changed since the last version;
2. navigate to the consequential sections;
3. trace important claims to sources or outputs;
4. distinguish stable content from provisional markers;
5. see unresolved decisions and constraints;
6. comment without creating competing authoritative copies; and
7. know what response will count as complete.

Use stable headings, line numbers or section identifiers. For code or analysis, include the input state, exact command or notebook, expected output and failing test. For a design decision, provide options and trade-offs—not only prose defending the preferred answer.

## Diagnose vague feedback

Translate the wording into a testable underlying issue:

| Comment | Possible underlying issue | Clarifying question |
|---|---|---|
| “Be more critical” | sources are summarised but not compared; warrants or contrary evidence are missing | Which claim most needs comparison or challenge? |
| “Needs more literature” | central claim lacks support, a field is missing or the boundary is unclear | Which decision or claim is currently unsupported? |
| “This doesn't flow” | paragraph functions, order or transitions are unclear | Where did the argument become difficult to follow? |
| “Do more analysis” | uncertainty or alternative explanation remains unresolved | What inference would the proposed analysis change? |
| “Simplify” | scope, terminology or sentence load exceeds the reader's need | Which idea or audience should govern the simplification? |

Do not pretend to understand a consequential comment. Paraphrase the issue, propose a response and ask for correction.

## Process feedback in a response matrix

For each substantive comment:

1. preserve the comment or a faithful summary;
2. identify the underlying concern;
3. classify it as accept, adapt, investigate, discuss or decline;
4. state the proposed response and rationale;
5. link the changed location or evidence;
6. identify effects elsewhere in the project; and
7. mark completion only after verification.

Comments can reveal a real problem while suggesting the wrong solution. “Add 20 citations” may signal that a central claim is ungrounded; narrowing the claim and adding three directly relevant sources may be a better response. Record why.

## Resolve conflicting feedback

When reviewers disagree:

1. state each recommendation faithfully;
2. identify whether they answer the same question and assume the same audience;
3. locate the actual decision and its owner;
4. compare options against contribution, evidence, method, genre, feasibility and formal requirements;
5. propose a resolution;
6. ask reviewers to discuss the unresolved decision together where useful; and
7. record the decision and downstream changes.

Do not silently implement the last or most senior comment merely to end discomfort. Do not triangulate supervisors through separate messages. If the disagreement concerns safety, integrity, approvals, authorship, discrimination or supervision breakdown, use independent specialist or formal support.

## Worked example: “rewrite the discussion”

**Material:** Full discussion draft, 4,200 words.

**Original request:** “Could you give feedback?”

**Responses:** Supervisor A says the chapter needs a stronger practical recommendation. Supervisor B says the design cannot support recommendations and asks for a complete rewrite.

**Underlying decision:** What strength of implication can the evidence support?

**Audit:** The study is cross-sectional, the outcome is self-reported and subgroup estimates are imprecise. The current draft uses causal language and recommends implementation.

**Options:** Remove the recommendation; reframe it as a hypothesis for prospective evaluation; or add evidence from another study if it genuinely supports the action. More confident wording is not an option.

**Provisional response:** Accept the inferential concern, revise causal statements, distinguish observed association from proposed mechanism, and state a bounded implication for future evaluation. Ask both supervisors whether this resolves the disagreement before sentence-level editing.

**Evidence of done:** Claim audit completed; discussion and abstract aligned; response matrix links every changed passage; both reviewers' unresolved objections recorded; final decision entered in the decision log.

## Protect independence while using expertise

Independence is not refusing help. It is increasingly being able to:

- diagnose the underlying problem;
- seek the right expertise;
- compare advice with evidence and requirements;
- propose and justify a response;
- implement it accurately; and
- explain the remaining uncertainty.

Supervisors remain responsible for their roles, and students should not be abandoned under the label of independence. Conversely, a reviewer rewriting every sentence can obscure whether the student understands the argument and can create attribution or authorship questions. Agree what kind of intervention is appropriate.

## When feedback is late

Record the agreed review window, its dependency and the decision date. Follow up with the exact material and requested decision. If delay threatens a milestone or repeats despite agreed arrangements, bring the record, impact, feasible alternatives and requested resolution to the appropriate supervision or graduate research process.

Do not describe a document as approved because no response arrived. Silence is not acceptance.

## Why feedback arrives late or misses the point

- sending an unlabeled file with “thoughts?”;
- requesting conceptual, methodological and copy feedback at once;
- asking after sending whether the reviewer has capacity;
- hiding known gaps that change how the draft should be read;
- distributing several competing copies;
- treating every comment as a literal instruction;
- dismissing a comment because its proposed solution is weak;
- resolving conflicts by hierarchy without examining the decision;
- marking a comment done when text changed but the issue remains;
- failing to update the abstract, methods or other linked sections;
- repeatedly sending unreconciled drafts; and
- treating silence as approval.

## When the work is ready to send for review

Work is reviewable when the reviewer can identify its purpose, state and decision; central evidence is inspectable; gaps are visible; the request fits the agreed time; and there is one authoritative response record. A developmental draft need not be polished, but it must be coherent enough for the requested judgement.

## Make one precise request of the reviewer

Bring:

- the exact version and review level;
- a concise cover note;
- one to three priority questions;
- changes since the previous review;
- known gaps and checks completed;
- the dependency and decision date; and
- the location of the response matrix and authoritative draft.

## Check the review contract before sharing

- [ ] The requested review level matches the draft state.
- [ ] The exact version and authoritative location are clear.
- [ ] The reviewer knows the audience and decision.
- [ ] Priority questions and exclusions are explicit.
- [ ] The requested scope fits the agreed review window.
- [ ] Central evidence and changes are inspectable.
- [ ] Feedback is translated into underlying issues.
- [ ] Every substantive comment has a reasoned disposition.
- [ ] Conflicts have an owner and documented resolution path.
- [ ] Completion is verified across linked sections and records.

## Source note

The review-level and response-matrix system is an editorial workflow. The distinction among goals, current performance and actionable next steps is informed by broader educational feedback research, whose effects are heterogeneous and not doctorate-specific [@hattie-timperley-2007; @wisniewski2020feedback].
